paper.title: Competitor phenology as a social cue in breeding site selection

experiment.manipulation: resident great-tit and blue-tit hatching phenology advanced versus delayed at forest-plot level
experiment.allocation: random assignment in two consecutive years with treatment swapping between years in reused sites

male_settlement_treatment_effect.interpretation: male settlement among available boxes did not respond detectably to tit timing treatment; authors note almost all males settled before treatment became apparent

female_settlement_cox.interpretation: later in the season, males in delayed-tit plots remained unpaired disproportionately; treatment differences became more pronounced after early-treatment tits began hatching

payoff_b_mapping.early_commitment_anchor: males largely settled before manipulated tit hatching was observable and showed no detectable settlement response to treatment
payoff_b_mapping.post_arrival_information_anchor: later-arriving females preferentially settled with males in earlier-tit plots, with treatment separation increasing later in the season
payoff_b_mapping.key_distinction: information availability depends on decision timing; arrival timing and settlement information use are separable
payoff_b_mapping.not_claimed: the experiment does not identify whether females used tit phenology directly versus correlated resource, predation, or competition information

claim_boundary: published-result anchor rather than a new PAYOFF-B reanalysis
female arrival timing itself was not experimentally caused by information availability
sex differences in waiting cost are a PAYOFF-B interpretation, not a measured parameter in the source paper
the exact sensory or ecological mechanism producing the social cue is unresolved by the original experiment
full Dryad-byte reanalysis remains pending authenticated file access
